newsitem.title: FRANCE: Angry Euro-MPs accuse Commission of dirty tactics.
newsitem.headline: Angry Euro-MPs accuse Commission of dirty tactics.

text.p: Euro-MPs accused the European Commission on Friday of trying to railroad through the Council a deal on fur imports from countries which use leghold traps, even though EU environment ministers have already rejected it.

"This displays contempt for the competence of the Environment Council," the European Parliament said in a resolution which called the steel-jawed traps "an unacceptable and cruel way of trapping animals".

The Commission has asked European Union foreign ministers meeting in Brussels next Monday to approve a draft deal reached with Canada and Russia on December 6, 1996, which sets so-called "humane" standards for trapping animals for their fur.

The Commission, Canada, the U.S. and Russia have been trying for months to agree on improved trapping methods in an attempt to ward off an outright EU ban on fur imports from these countries, where the leghold trap is still used.
The three nations have threatened trade sanctions against the EU if the ban, agreed in 1991 but never implemented, goes ahead.
EU environment ministers last December dismissed the draft deal with Canada and Russia (rejected by Washington) out of concern that it "would allow some form of leghold traps to continue to be used".
Commissioner Papoutsis raised the hackles of Euro-MPs on Friday by calling the environment ministers' stance a "delay".

Euro-MPs from across the political spectrum insisted the only solution that would satisfy parliament and ministers was a complete ban on the traps, which do not kill animals outright but often imprison them until they bleed or starve to death, or bite off their trapped limb to escape.
In an angry debate, Euro-MPs accused the Commission of lying about its intentions and putting trade interests above democratic principles and animal welfare.
British Socialist Anita Pollack said the Commission was wrong to bow to pressure from the Canadians and their allies.
It was not a foregone conclusion that these countries would win a challenge to the EU fur ban at the World Trade Organisation (WTO), she argued.
They could not claim the ban gave the EU an unfair trade advantage since sixty other fur trading nations had already outlawed leghold traps.
And in addition, WTO rules allowed exemptions to free trade when this was necessary to protect public morals, Pollack said.

Veteran German Christian Democrat Otto von Hapsburg, himself a hunter, said proposed variations to the leghold trap, such as covering its steel jaws with rubber strips, did not make it any more humane and urged the Commission to implement the ban now.
"We do not want any more words. We want action," he said.
